hints: Compare the three curves in two ways: how steep they are at the start (0 to 10 minutes) and how high they finish (the flat plateau level).
Remember that steepness shows initial rate, while plateau height shows total amount of product made. A low, early plateau with the same starting starch suggests the enzyme stopped working.
walkthrough:
**Read what the axes tell us**

Hello, let's look together. The y-axis is concentration of reducing sugar, so this is product made from starch by amylase.

The steeper the curve, the faster the rate. The higher the final flat part (plateau), the more total starch was hydrolysed.

**Compare rate and total product**

At 70 °C the curve starts steepest, so the initial rate is actually fastest. But it plateaus earliest and lowest.

At 50 °C the curve starts slowest, but it keeps rising longest and finishes highest. All tubes started with the same concentration and volume of starch.

**Explain the low plateau at high temperature**

If the enzyme kept working, all three tubes should reach the same final sugar concentration because they started with the same starch.

The fact that 70 °C and 60 °C stop lower means the reaction stopped early. The best explanation is the enzyme was denatured by heat before all substrate was used up, most severely at 70 °C.

options.A: 50 °C gives the most product here, but only three temperatures were tested. You cannot claim it is the optimum without testing temperatures above and below.
options.B: At 60 °C the curve plateaus below the 50 °C curve, so less sugar was made. That means not all starch was hydrolysed.
options.C: At 70 °C the reaction stops very early at the lowest plateau despite the same starting starch. This shows the amylase lost its shape and function before finishing hydrolysis.
options.D: The initial gradient is steepest at 70 °C, so initial rate is faster at 70 °C than at 50 °C. Option D reverses this.
